clue.text: One who must keep mum after a second hitch occurs

definitions.text: One who must keep mum after a second hitch occurs

parts.words: One who must keep mum after a second hitch occurs
parts.note: read 'keep mum' as supporting a mother rather than staying quiet, and 'hitch' as getting married: the man a mother weds the second time round

explanation.surface: Someone sworn to secrecy once a second snag crops up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep mum' seems to mean stay silent, and 'hitch' a snag; really they are providing for a mother and getting hitched, i.e. married.
explanation.definitionFit: A mother's second husband becomes the stepparent who helps support her household.

clue.text: Heard to drive away in an Oxford, perhaps

indicators.note: heard tells us the word for chasing off is only spoken, so we write a word that sounds the same

parts.note: to shoo is to drive away an animal or person with a cry

explanation.surface: Something overheard about leaving Oxford by car.
explanation.walkthrough: An Oxford is not the city here but a style of laced leather shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oxford is a classic laced leather style of footwear, so it is one example.

clue.text: Join coach in quarters to prepare for races

parts.note: E and N are two compass points, or quarters
athletes train to get ready for races

explanation.surface: Hiring a coach to live with you while getting ready for athletics meetings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' looks like a trainer, but it is a railway carriage you board.
explanation.definitionFit: To board a railway carriage is to get onto a train, so it means joining a coach.

clue.text: Professor who joined up to make himself a man

definitions.text: Professor who joined up to make himself a man

parts.words: Professor who joined up to make himself a man
parts.note: 'joined up' suggests enlisting to prove one's manhood, but it describes a scientist stitching body parts together to build a man

explanation.surface: An academic who enlisted in the army to grow up.
explanation.walkthrough: Joining up sounds like enlisting; in the novel by Mary Shelley the scientist joins up parts of corpses to make a creature.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Shelley's scientist assembles a creature from body parts, literally joining up a human figure.

clue.text: State of panic follows constricted position at chess

parts.note: to tail someone is to follow them, so tails means follows
a pin in chess is a piece trapped because moving it would expose a more valuable one

explanation.surface: Fear sets in after being trapped in a chess game.
explanation.definitionFit: A plane's uncontrolled spiralling dive gives the figurative sense of a panicky collapse.

clue.text: Group of nine or ten one had be headed

indicators.note: be headed (beheaded) tells us each of the three words loses its first letter

explanation.surface: A party of nine or ten people, one of whom was executed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'be headed' is the newspaper's split of 'beheaded', which tells us to drop each word's opening letter; 'or ten' makes the group look loosely counted.
explanation.definitionFit: From the Greek for nine, the word names a set of nine things.

clue.text: Sign showing old people

parts.note: men means people in general

explanation.surface: A notice that displays elderly folk.
explanation.definitionFit: A portent is a sign of what is to come.

clue.text: Poet favouring clashes between lines?

definitions.meaning: the Roman epigram writer Marcus Valerius Martialis
warlike, keen on battles between opposing battle lines

explanation.walkthrough: The 'lines' sound poetic, after 'Poet', but they are lines of soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: Warlike or military in spirit, fond of fighting between armies; also the name of a Latin epigrammatist.

clue.text: Dress for retirement, almost casual wear

parts.note: nigh means nearly, almost
a T-shirt is informal clothing

explanation.surface: Clothes for leaving work: nearly always informal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retirement' is not leaving work but retiring to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Retiring here means going to bed, and this garment is worn in bed.

clue.text: Someone who comes in for special treatment

definitions.text: Someone who comes in for special treatment

parts.words: Someone who comes in for special treatment
parts.note: 'comes in for' suggests receiving favours, but read literally it is a person visiting a hospital for treatment without staying overnight

explanation.surface: A favoured person who gets extra attention.
explanation.definitionFit: A hospital visitor treated without being admitted to a ward arrives, is seen, and goes home.

clue.text: Warder going round misses a narcotic

indicators.note: misses tells us a letter is dropped from what we have built
going round tells us the warder's word is turned to run in the other direction

parts.note: a guard is a prison warder

explanation.surface: A prison officer on patrol fails to spot a narcotic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going round' turns GUARD into DRAUG; 'misses a' removes its A.
explanation.definitionFit: A narcotic is one kind of illicit substance or medicine.

clue.text: Amount of energy initially extracted from buckwheat?

definitions.text: Amount of energy initially extracted from buckwheat?

parts.words: Amount of energy initially extracted from buckwheat?
parts.note: 'initially' points to an abbreviation in initials, and the unit's short form kWh sits inside the word buckwheat

explanation.surface: How much energy you could get from a cereal crop.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters kWh, the initials of the unit, are found inside bucKWHeat; the whole is a cryptic definition rather than a standard hidden word.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a unit of electrical energy: one thousand watts used for sixty minutes.

clue.text: Wolves prepare for an away visit

definitions.meaning: a group of wolves hunting together
to put clothes into a suitcase before travelling

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wolves' looks like a football team heading for an away match; it is a hunting group.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of wolves is a hunting band; getting ready for a trip means filling a suitcase.

clue.text: Communist disrupted last sit-in

indicators.note: disrupted tells us the letters of the words that follow are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A party member broke up the most recent occupation protest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disrupted' rearranges LAST and SITIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of the Soviet leader's hard-line version of communism.

clue.text: Thief holding up store?

parts.note: 'holding up' suggests armed robbery, but it is a light-fingered person who lifts goods from a retail outlet

explanation.surface: A robber staging a hold-up at a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Holding up a store sounds like armed robbery; read literally it is someone lifting goods in a store.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who steals goods from a retail outlet while posing as a customer.

clue.text: Use hammer on swing, getting minor injury to hand

indicators.note: on tells us the hammering word comes placed after the swinging word

parts.note: to hang is to swing, as from a rope
to nail something is to use a hammer on it

explanation.surface: Hammering on a swing and hurting a finger.
explanation.definitionFit: A painful torn strip of skin beside a fingernail is a small injury to the hand.

clue.text: Low note for brass

parts.note: to low is to moo like cattle
lah is the sixth note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A deep musical note played on a brass instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' looks like the instrument section, but is British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are slang words for money.

clue.text: Mark one third of league position here

parts.note: a league is an old measure of three miles
a post is a position or job

explanation.surface: Marking a third of the way through the league season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'League' looks like a sports competition, but it is a distance of three miles; 'here' links the wordplay to the marker.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadside marker showing distance travelled.

clue.text: Equality one found 'in Labour, perhaps

indicators.note: found in tells us one piece is located inside another

parts.note: the Labour Party is one example of a political party
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Fairness is something the Labour movement might be found to hold.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on an equal footing is equivalence or sameness of status.

clue.text: Blame drink for state of relationship

parts.note: to take the rap is to take the blame
port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: Blaming alcohol for how a romance is going.
explanation.definitionFit: Good understanding and harmony between people describes how they get on.

clue.text: A magistracy in Australia turned up for him

definitions.text: A magistracy in Australia turned up for him

parts.words: A magistracy in Australia turned up for him
parts.note: the optimistic Dickens character always waiting for something to turn up ends David Copperfield as a magistrate in Australia

explanation.surface: A man who stumbled into a judicial post down under.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dickens character's catchphrase is that something will turn up; at the end of David Copperfield he becomes a magistrate in Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: The ever-hopeful debtor in Dickens finally finds a post as a colonial magistrate.

clue.text: Route worker takes home from plant

annotationWithheld.why: Route worker takes home from plant (7): BEE (worker) is clear, but no parse of 'takes home from plant' gives LINE; possibly an OCR misreading, and a search of the exact text found nothing
annotationWithheld.clue: Route worker takes home from plant

clue.text: Writer's block ruling out completion

definitions.note: Writer's here reads as writer is, the 's being a link

indicators.note: ruling out completion tells us the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: a barrier is a block or obstruction

explanation.surface: An author's inability to finish a piece of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer's block' reads as a phrase; split, it is the Peter Pan author J M Barrie and a barrier missing its end.
explanation.definitionFit: J M Barrie was the Scottish author of Peter Pan.

clue.text: Confidentially, not a rank outsider?

definitions.meaning: someone inside the lowest army rank, rather than outside it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank outsider' suggests a long shot in a race; here rank is military, the rank of private soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Done secretly, away from the public, matching confidentially; and literally a soldier in the lowest rank.

clue.text: Row when clock loses minutes

indicators.note: loses tells us something is taken away from the word for a clock

parts.note: a timer is a clock

explanation.surface: An argument when the clock runs slow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' suggests a quarrel, but it is a line or level of seats.
explanation.definitionFit: One level in a stepped arrangement, like a line of seats in a stadium.

clue.text: Top man among leading characters in The Sun Also Rises

indicators.note: leading characters in tells us to take the opening letter of each following word

explanation.surface: The hero of a Hemingway novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading characters' look like the novel's protagonists, but are the first letters of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian emperor was the ruler at the very top.

clue.text: Attempt to encircle old and historic city

indicators.note: to encircle tells us the attempt word surrounds the other piece

parts.note: a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: An effort to surround an ancient town.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient city of Homer's Iliad, besieged by the Greeks.

clue.text: Study of working efficiency making incomers go mad

indicators.note: mad tells us the letters of the words beside it are scrambled wildly

explanation.surface: Newcomers to a workplace become furious at a time-and-motion study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mad' rearranges INCOMERS and GO.
explanation.definitionFit: The science of designing workplaces and equipment so people work well and comfortably.

clue.text: Cobblers brought before a tribunal

parts.note: cobblers is British slang for nonsense, as is rot

explanation.surface: Shoemakers summoned before a court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cobblers' are not shoemakers but British slang for nonsense; the Rota is the Roman Catholic Church's supreme court.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rota is a court of appeal of the Roman Catholic Church.

clue.text: Almost starry-eyed, rambling about English past

indicators.note: about tells us the remaining letters go around another piece
rambling tells us the letters wander into a new order
almost tells us the final letter is cut from the word

parts.note: taken as written, without its hyphen

explanation.surface: Nearly dreamy and wandering on about England's history.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts the D from STARRYEYED; 'rambling' rearranges STARRYEYE, and 'about' puts it around E.
explanation.definitionFit: Times gone by, the past, especially as remembered with nostalgia.
